chunks: Why digital systems need clocks. The question: Why are clocks needed?
A clock is a signal that ticks at a steady rate, and digital circuits use the ticks to decide when to update.
Logic gates need a little time to settle on the right answer, and they can show wrong values on the way.
The clock says "capture now", so every memory element grabs its input at the same instant, after things have settled.
Picture a classroom where every student does scratch work and a bell rings at regular intervals. At each bell, everyone copies their current answer onto the board.
Between bells the scratch work can be as messy as it likes, because nobody reads it. Only what is on the board at the bell counts.
The catch: the time between bells must be long enough for the slowest student to finish.
When A falls, the AND term A·B falls at once but the other term rises one inverter delay later, so F glitches low (red) for one slot between two clock edges.
Q only samples F at the edges: just before the glitch and again after F has settled back to 1 (the setup margin is what guarantees it has settled).
The glitch itself is never captured. The clock decides when you look.
Clock period: the time between ticks. The frequency is 1 divided by the period.
Flip-flop: a one-bit memory that copies its input only at a clock tick ("How a flip-flop or latch works").
Combinational logic: gates whose output depends only on their current inputs, with no memory. Glitch: a brief wrong output while gates are still settling.
A block of logic needs 4 nanoseconds to settle, and the flip-flop adds about 0. 5 nanoseconds of its own delay. Choose a period of 5 nanoseconds, which is a 200 megahertz clock.
The output may glitch for the first 4 nanoseconds, but the flip-flop only looks at the 5 nanoseconds tick, when the answer is clean.
A 2 nanoseconds period would capture an unfinished answer. That is the whole idea: the clock turns messy, continuous change into clean steps.
"Logic takes time to settle and glitches on the way, so we need a point at which values are guaranteed valid.
The clock provides it: flip-flops capture on the edge, and between edges the logic can glitch freely.
That makes the design a simple state-to-next-state machine, lets us pipeline for speed, orders operations, and gives timers and protocols a time base.
The costs are clock power, skew and jitter, and EMI; the alternative is asynchronous design, which is harder."
